chunks: From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

So when a man is struck on the head and his tongue becomes heavy (stiff), the letters of the alphabet are presented to him. Whatever he fails to articulate clearly from them, he pays compensation for that portion of the alphabet. The original blood money is established upon the entire alphabet, then he is given [deducted] according to what he failed to articulate from them, and they are thirty-six letters.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or financial compensation for bodily injury or death
key_terms.اللِّسَانُ: The tongue, referring to the organ of speech
key_terms.حُرُوفُ الْمُعْجَمِ: The letters of the alphabet (specifically the 28 or 36 letters of Arabic)
key_terms.يُفْصِحْ: To articulate clearly or pronounce distinctly

ai.seo_question: How is the blood money for a damaged tongue calculated in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar details the jurisprudential calculation of *diyah* (blood money) for impaired speech, establishing that compensation is proportional to the specific Arabic letters (*huruf*) a victim fails to articulate clearly. It highlights the scholarly consensus on treating linguistic precision as a quantifiable bodily function, where the standard set of twenty-nine letters serves as the baseline for assessing the severity of the injury and determining the exact financial restitution.
